script.opening: (Mother, tired but brisk; Theo playing in the background.) "He's been pulling at his ear for a few days, then this morning there was yellowy gunk all over the pillow — his ear's been running. He's actually a bit brighter now the gunk's come out. But surely that means infection, so he needs antibiotics, right? I don't want it spreading."

facts.text: Runny nose and cough for 5 days, pulling at his right ear and grizzly for 3 days, poor sleep. Discharge from the right ear overnight — yellow, a bit smelly. "The pain seemed to go when the gunk came."
"He's had some breakfast and he's been playing with his cars." Alert, chatty, running around. Can bring him to the camera: pink, breathing normally, no rash.
"I haven't measured it today." Felt hot last night, 38.4°C at 2 am, Calpol given. "He's weeing normally." Drinking well. No vomiting or diarrhoea.

Behind the ear: "No, it looks the same as the other side" — no swelling, redness, or ear sticking out. "No, nothing like that" — no stiff neck, no rash, no headache, no drowsiness, no facial droop, no dizziness. Hearing a bit muffled on that side.
"No, nothing" — healthy, no previous ear infections or grommets, immunisations up to date, no allergies. Weight about 17 kg. Goes to nursery.
Calpol last night only. Hasn't given ibuprofen — "I didn't know I could give both."
Lives with Mum (Gemma, nursery nurse) and baby sister. Mum can bring him to the surgery today.

Worried, short of sleep, expecting antibiotics. If asked what she's worried about: "That the infection's got so bad it's bursting out. That it could go to his brain or something. I didn't sleep much either." Relieved by a clear explanation: "Oh. So it's not getting worse?" Given a choice, she would "prefer to start it" (antibiotic) — accepts a shared plan with a look in his ear first. If refused flatly without explanation, becomes cross: "So we just leave it?"

ice.ideas: "Gunk means infection, and infection needs antibiotics."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — fear the infection is "bursting out" and could spread to his brain; exhausted after a bad night.
ice.expectations: "Antibiotics, so it doesn't spread." Underneath: "I just want to do something."

cues: "He's actually a bit brighter." — the discharge relieved the pain.
"I don't want it spreading." — the fear to explore.
"I just want to do something." — invites a practical plan (pain relief).

checkpoints.text: Assesses the child as well vs unwell FIRST (temperature, systemic state, feeding/fluids, NICE NG143 traffic-light) and arranges a face-to-face examination of ears/throat/chest, as otoscopy cannot be done by video — not assuming severity from the discharge
Explains the discharge correctly — otorrhoea in AOM usually means a perforation that relieves pain and generally heals — defusing the "running ear = serious" fear

Applies NICE NG91 antibiotic STEWARDSHIP: knows most AOM is self-limiting, that an immediate antibiotic is for the systemically very unwell, complications or high risk, and that for <2 with bilateral AOM or AOM with otorrhoea no, back-up or immediate antibiotic are all options — so a shared decision here, made on assessment not reflex

Emphasises ANALGESIA as the mainstay (regular paracetamol/ibuprofen at the dose for age or weight, often under-used; no anaesthetic drops with a perforation) and explains the natural course (keep ear dry, perforation heals)
SAFETY-NETS for complications — mastoiditis, meningitis, worsening/high fever, facial weakness, persistent discharge/hearing loss — with plain-language red flags
Manages the parental antibiotic EXPECTATION with explanation and partnership rather than confrontation or a reflexive prescription
Reassures the worried mother (bad night, fear of spreading) and checks her understanding of the plan
Safety-nets and follows up: clear red flags and when to seek urgent help, analgesia plan, expected recovery, and review if not settling/persistent discharge — evidence-based, stewardship-minded care

worked.txt: "Let me check him over first — how he’s feeding and playing, and bring him close to the camera for me. … He’s actually pretty well in himself, which is reassuring. I can’t look inside his ears on video, so I’d like to see him this afternoon to check his ears, throat and temperature."
"That ‘gunk’ is usually a sign the eardrum has let go a little to release the pressure — which is exactly why his pain eased. It looks dramatic but it’s common and the drum heals itself."

"On antibiotics — most ear infections actually get better on their own, so we don’t always use them. But because his ear is discharging, this is one of the situations where antibiotics help more often, so no antibiotic, one to keep in reserve, or one to start now are all reasonable — let’s decide together once I’ve looked. The key, though, is regular pain relief."

"Give paracetamol or ibuprofen regularly at the right dose for his age or weight — that’s what makes him comfortable. Keep the ear dry, don’t poke anything in it, and no numbing ear drops while it’s discharging."

"Come back urgently if he becomes very unwell, gets swelling or redness behind the ear or it sticks out, a high fever, a stiff neck, a rash that doesn’t fade, or he’s drowsy — those are the things we never want to miss."
"The discharge should settle over a few days and the drum heal over a few weeks. If it keeps running, his hearing seems off, or he’s not improving, bring him back so we can check it."

f.learning: A discharging ear in a child is usually acute otitis media with a perforated eardrum: the otorrhoea releases pus and characteristically relieves the pain (hence the child being "brighter"), it looks alarming but is common and usually self-limiting, and the perforation typically heals — so assess the child as well versus unwell first (temperature, systemic state, feeding/fluids, NICE NG143 traffic-light, with a face-to-face ear/throat/chest examination because otoscopy cannot be done by video) rather than assuming severity from the discharge. Apply NICE NG91 antibiotic stewardship: most acute otitis media resolves without antibiotics and many children need only analgesia or a back-up (delayed) prescription; an immediate antibiotic is for the systemically very unwell, features of a serious illness/complication, or high risk of complications, while for children under 2 with bilateral AOM and AOM with otorrhoea (discharge) NG91 advises considering no antibiotic, a back-up or an immediate antibiotic — so this child, with a discharging ear, falls into a group where all three are reasonable, with the decision shared with the parent, made on assessment and with stewardship, not reflexively (if used, amoxicillin for 5–7 days, dose per BNFC). Emphasise analgesia as the mainstay (regular weight-based paracetamol/ibuprofen, frequently under-used), explain the natural course (keep the ear dry, the drum heals), and avoid decongestants/antihistamines and anaesthetic ear drops (phenazone with lidocaine) when the drum is perforated or the ear is discharging. Safety-net explicitly for the rare serious complications — mastoiditis (swelling/redness behind the ear, the pinna pushed forward), meningitis (very unwell, neck stiffness, photophobia, non-blanching rash, drowsiness), worsening or high fever, facial weakness, and persistent discharge/hearing loss — with plain-language red flags. The hidden agenda is parental worry and a belief that discharge means a serious spreading infection needing antibiotics; manage that expectation with explanation and partnership, using this as a teachable shared decision rather than a flat refusal or a reflexive prescription.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG91 (2018, updated 2022) — Otitis media (acute): antimicrobial prescribing · NICE NG143 (2019) — Fever in under 5s · NICE NG240 (2024) — Meningitis (bacterial) and meningococcal disease
knowledge.summary: A discharging ear after a few days of earache is usually acute otitis media with a perforated drum. Assess well versus unwell first. Under NICE NG91, otorrhoea is one of the groups where an antibiotic is more likely to help, so no, back-up or immediate antibiotic are all reasonable options, chosen with the parent.

points.t: Temperature, colour, activity, hydration and breathing using the NICE NG143 traffic-light table in a febrile child under 5. Brighter, eating and playing is reassuring. Otoscopy is needed to confirm the diagnosis, so a video assessment is followed by a face-to-face examination.
Pain that eases suddenly as discharge appears suggests the drum has perforated and released pus. The perforation usually heals once the infection settles; recheck it if discharge persists.

NICE NG91: most children improve within about 3 days without antibiotics, though it can last up to a week. Offer paracetamol or ibuprofen at the dose for age or weight (BNFC). Anaesthetic ear drops (phenazone with lidocaine) are not used when the drum is perforated or the ear is discharging.

Immediate antibiotic for the systemically very unwell, signs of a more serious illness, or high risk of complications. For otorrhoea, or under 2 with both ears affected, consider no, back-up or immediate antibiotic — these groups benefit more. Otherwise no antibiotic or a back-up to use if not improving within 3 days or worse at any time.
NICE NG91: amoxicillin for 5 to 7 days, dose by age per NG91 and BNFC. Penicillin allergy: clarithromycin. Co-amoxiclav is the second choice if symptoms worsen after 2 to 3 days of the first choice.

NICE NG91: refer to hospital for a severe systemic infection or an acute complication — mastoiditis, meningitis, intracranial abscess, sinus thrombosis or facial nerve paralysis. Meningitis features follow NICE NG240; a febrile child with red features follows NICE NG143.

dg.d: Open question to mother; noticed the child on screen; let her describe the pillow, the few days of earache and the antibiotic request in her own words.
Bad night, parental exhaustion and the wish to “do something”; can she attend in person today.
NG143 traffic-light features by video, then face-to-face otoscopy, throat, chest and temperature; no swab needed routinely.
AOM with perforation versus otitis externa, and complications (mastoiditis, meningitis, facial palsy).
Checked behind the ear, neck stiffness, drowsiness, rash, facial weakness, hydration and breathing.
Acute otitis media with probable perforation in a systemically well child, confirmed on examination.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: NG91 options for otorrhoea explained; shared decision on amoxicillin 5 to 7 days if confirmed; regular analgesia; keep the ear dry.
Checked allergy and high-risk conditions before prescribing; no decongestants, antihistamines or anaesthetic drops with a perforation.
999 features, same-day features, review if not improving in 2 to 3 days, and recheck the drum if discharge persists.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “he’s brighter now” as the key clinical cue and “I don’t want it spreading” as the key emotional cue, and explored both.
Idea (running ear = spreading infection); concern (it reaching his brain); expectation (antibiotics today).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — fear the infection is "bursting out" and could spread to his brain; exhausted after a bad night — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, thanks for calling in — and hello Theo, I can see you there. Tell me what’s been happening, from the start.
model.why: Open question to the parent, and includes the child

model.text: He’s been pulling at his ear for a few days with a cold, then this morning there was yellow gunk all over his pillow. He’s actually brighter now it’s come out. But that’s infection, isn’t it? He needs antibiotics — I don’t want it spreading.

That sounds like a rough night, and I can see why the pillow gave you a fright. I do want to answer the antibiotic question properly. First I’d like a few questions about how he is in himself, then I’ll explain what I think is going on, and we’ll decide together. Is that alright?
model.why: Acknowledges the worry and sets a clear structure

model.text: Yes, fine.
You said he’s brighter. What’s he doing this morning — is he eating, drinking, playing?
model.why: Starts the well-versus-unwell assessment with function, not the discharge

model.text: He’s had some breakfast and he’s been playing with his cars. The pain seemed to go when the gunk came.
That pattern helps a lot. Has he had a high temperature? And is he weeing as usual, with wet nappies or trips to the toilet?
I haven’t measured it today. He’s weeing normally.

Could you bring him close to the camera for me? … Good colour, he’s chatting, his breathing looks easy. Theo, can you show me which ear was sore? … Mum, is there any swelling, redness or tenderness behind that ear, or does the ear look pushed forward?
model.why: Remote observation plus a targeted mastoiditis check

model.text: No, it looks the same as the other side.
And any headache, stiff neck, being unusually sleepy, a rash, or any drooping of his face?
model.why: Screens for meningitis and facial nerve palsy

model.text: No, nothing like that.
Does he have any other health problems, or any allergy to medicines? Nothing is recorded on his notes.
model.why: Checks high-risk comorbidity and allergy before any prescription

model.text: No, nothing.
You mentioned it spreading. What were you picturing when you saw the pillow?
model.why: Explores the specific fear behind the antibiotic request

model.text: That the infection’s got so bad it’s bursting out. That it could go to his brain or something. I didn’t sleep much either.
That’s a very natural thing to think when you see it, especially after a bad night. So your main hope today is something to stop it getting worse — is that fair?
Yes. I just want to do something.

Here’s what I think. The cold has blocked the tube behind his eardrum and it filled with infected fluid — a middle-ear infection. The pressure built up, the drum let go a tiny bit, and the fluid came out. That’s why his pain went and he perked up. It looks dramatic, but it’s common, and the small hole almost always heals on its own.
model.why: Explains perforation and otorrhoea in plain language

model.text: Oh. So it’s not getting worse?

From what I can see, he’s a well boy. I can’t look inside his ear on a video, though, and I want to do that — can you bring him in this afternoon so I can check his ears, throat and chest and take his temperature?
model.why: Recognises the limits of video; arranges the examination the diagnosis needs

model.text: Yes, I can do that.

On antibiotics: most ear infections get better within about three days without them. But a discharging ear is one of the situations where antibiotics help more often, so the national guidance says it’s reasonable either way — no antibiotic, one to keep in reserve, or one to start now. If the examination fits, I’m happy to start amoxicillin today, since that’s what you’d prefer. Whatever we decide, the thing that makes him comfortable is pain relief.
model.why: Applies NG91 accurately for otorrhoea and makes it a shared decision

model.text: I would prefer to start it, yes. What about the pain relief?

Paracetamol, or ibuprofen, at the dose on the packet for his age, given regularly while he’s sore rather than only when he cries. Keep water out of that ear — no swimming, and a cotton-wool plug smeared with Vaseline in the bath — and don’t poke anything in to clean it. Just wipe the outside.
model.why: Analgesia as the mainstay, plus practical care of a perforated ear

model.text: Okay. How long will the gunk keep coming?
Usually a few days. If it keeps running once the infection has settled, or you think his hearing isn’t right once he’s better, I’ll want to look again to check the drum has healed.
model.why: Sets the expected course and a follow-up trigger

model.text: That makes sense.
Can I check it makes sense to you too? When someone at home asks what the doctor said, what will you tell them?
That his eardrum burst to let the pressure out, which is why he’s better, and it’ll heal. Regular Calpol or ibuprofen, keep it dry, and maybe antibiotics after you’ve looked.

Perfect. Now the important part. Call 999 or go to A&E if he becomes very drowsy or hard to wake, has a stiff neck, a rash that doesn’t fade under a glass, or is struggling to breathe. Come back the same day if a swelling or redness appears behind the ear or the ear sticks out, his face droops, he has a high temperature that won’t settle, or he stops drinking.
model.why: Specific plain-language red flags for meningitis, mastoiditis and facial palsy

model.text: Behind the ear, stiff neck, rash, face — got it.

And if the antibiotic has been started and he’s not getting better after two or three days, ring us. You did the right thing calling. I’ll see you both this afternoon — anything else before we finish?
model.why: Affirms the parent and closes with a clear plan

model.text: No, that’s really helpful. Thank you.

social.t: A frightening night drives the request. Acknowledging exhaustion and the wish to act builds trust faster than facts alone.
Keeping the ear dry (no swimming, care at bath time) and not cleaning inside the canal are practical points parents often miss.

legal.t: GMC Good practice in proposing, prescribing, providing and managing medicines and devices (2021): prescribe remotely only when you have enough information to do so safely; otherwise arrange an examination.

professional.t: NICE NG91 sets out when antibiotics help in acute otitis media. Following it — and explaining it — is good practice rather than rationing.
GMC Decision making and consent (2020): where more than one option is reasonable, share the choice with the parent and record the discussion and safety-net.

community.t: Pharmacists can advise on paracetamol and ibuprofen dosing for age and weight, and on when to seek further help.

redFlags: Swelling, redness or tenderness behind the ear, or the ear pushed forward (mastoiditis) — hospital
Drowsiness, neck stiffness, non-blanching rash, very unwell (meningitis) — 999
Facial weakness, or NG143 red traffic-light features in a febrile child under 5
psychosocial: A disturbed night for the whole family and an exhausted parent
Practical ability to attend today for examination
Past experience that may have taught her that discharge means antibiotics
ice: Idea: “A running ear means the infection is bursting out”
Concern: “It could spread to his brain”

playbook.diagnosis: Acute otitis media with a probable perforated eardrum in a systemically well child. Confirm with otoscopy; NICE NG91 lists otorrhoea as a group where no, back-up or immediate antibiotic are all reasonable.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “The cold blocked the tube behind his eardrum and it filled with infected fluid. The pressure made a tiny hole in the drum, the fluid came out, and that’s why the pain eased. The hole almost always heals by itself.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried it was spreading — actually the discharge is his ear letting the pressure out, which is why he perked up. We’ll still keep a close eye for the rare signs that it is spreading.”
management.psychosocial: Acknowledge the bad night and the wish to do something; make the antibiotic decision together so mother leaves with a plan she owns, and arrange a convenient time for the examination.
sharedPlan: Face-to-face examination today: otoscopy, throat, chest, temperature
NG91 shared decision — amoxicillin 5 to 7 days if confirmed and chosen (dose by age per BNFC)
Regular paracetamol or ibuprofen; keep the ear dry; nothing inside the canal
safetyNet: 999: drowsy, stiff neck, non-blanching rash, breathing difficulty
Same day: swelling behind the ear, facial droop, persistent high fever, not drinking
Review if not improving in 2 to 3 days, or discharge or hearing concern persists

pitfalls.intro: This station tests whether you can make an evidence-based antibiotic decision with a worried parent, not whether you know amoxicillin. Candidates fail it by refusing, by prescribing reflexively, or by forgetting that a video call cannot look inside an ear.

items.fail: Telling mother that antibiotics are never needed for ear infections.
items.why: NICE NG91 names otorrhoea as a group where antibiotics are more likely to help. A flat refusal is inaccurate management as well as poor relating.
items.fix: State the nuance: “Most ear infections settle alone, but with a discharging ear an antibiotic is a reasonable choice — let’s decide together.”

items.fail: Prescribing on the strength of “yellow gunk” without asking how the child is or arranging an examination.
items.why: “Did not assess the severity of illness” and “inadequate data gathering” are standard failing statements. Otitis externa and complications look different on examination.
items.fix: Ask about eating, drinking, playing and weeing, observe on camera, check behind the ear, then arrange same-day otoscopy.

items.fail: Treating “I don’t want it spreading” as a demand and answering it with statistics.
items.why: The fear of spread is the emotional hinge. Unexplored, it resurfaces as persistent requests however good the explanation.
items.fix: “What were you picturing when you saw the pillow?” — then explain the perforation as the answer to that fear.

items.fail: No pain-relief advice, or advising anaesthetic ear drops for a discharging ear.
items.why: NICE NG91 puts analgesia first, and phenazone with lidocaine drops are only for an intact drum without otorrhoea.
items.fix: Regular paracetamol or ibuprofen at the dose for age, dry-ear advice, nothing inside the canal.

items.fail: Closing with “come back if he gets worse”.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting fails the Global Skills domain; mastoiditis and meningitis are the complications examiners expect you to name.
items.fix: Name the signs: swelling behind the ear, a stiff neck, a rash that doesn’t fade, very drowsy, a drooping face — and give a review point at 2 to 3 days.

items.fail: Spending eight minutes on ear history and never reaching the decision.
items.why: “Management plan insufficiently developed” is the commonest reason for failing a station.
items.fix: Have the well/unwell picture by minute 4 and be explaining by minute 6.

Eating, drinking, playing, weeing, temperature, breathing, colour on camera. Behind the ear, stiff neck, rash, drowsiness, facial droop. Allergy and comorbidity.
What did she picture when she saw the pillow? Name the fear of spread before you explain anything.

wordPics.fail: Prescribes over video without any well/unwell assessment, or refuses flatly and lectures on resistance; never explains the discharge; no pain-relief advice; no mention of mastoiditis or meningitis; mother leaves still believing the infection is “bursting out”.
wordPics.pass: Assesses the child’s function and red flags, arranges examination, explains that the discharge means a perforation, makes an NG91-consistent antibiotic decision, advises regular analgesia and gives a basic safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: uses “he’s brighter” to reassure; states accurately that otorrhoea is a group where no, back-up or immediate antibiotic are all reasonable and lets mother share the choice; recognises what video cannot do; gives specific, memorable red flags and a clear review point; mother feels heard, not judged.

avoid.dont: “Antibiotics don’t work for ear infections — they get better on their own.”
avoid.instead: “Most ear infections settle by themselves, but a discharging ear is one where antibiotics help more often — so let’s decide together once I’ve looked.”
avoid.why: A blanket refusal is both confrontational and inaccurate for otorrhoea under NICE NG91.

avoid.dont: “Pus coming out means a nasty infection, so we’ll start antibiotics straight away.”
avoid.instead: “The discharge usually means the eardrum has released the pressure — that’s why he feels better.”
avoid.why: It confirms the mother’s fear and skips the assessment that the prescription should rest on.

avoid.instead: “Swelling behind the ear, a stiff neck, a rash that doesn’t fade, or very drowsy — that’s urgent.”
avoid.why: Non-specific safety-netting earns no credit; named complications do.

SCA_MODELS.text: Oh. So it’s not getting worse?

From what I can see, he’s a well boy. I can’t look inside his ear on a video, though, and I want to do that — can you bring him in this afternoon so I can check his ears, throat and chest and take his temperature?
SCA_MODELS.why: Recognises the limits of video; arranges the examination the diagnosis needs

SCA_MODELS.text: Yes, I can do that.

On antibiotics: most ear infections get better within about three days without them. But a discharging ear is one of the situations where antibiotics help more often, so the national guidance says it’s reasonable either way — no antibiotic, one to keep in reserve, or one to start now. If the examination fits, I’m happy to start amoxicillin today, since that’s what you’d prefer. Whatever we decide, the thing that makes him comfortable is pain relief.
SCA_MODELS.why: Applies NG91 accurately for otorrhoea and makes it a shared decision

SCA_MODELS.text: I would prefer to start it, yes. What about the pain relief?

Paracetamol, or ibuprofen, at the dose on the packet for his age, given regularly while he’s sore rather than only when he cries. Keep water out of that ear — no swimming, and a cotton-wool plug smeared with Vaseline in the bath — and don’t poke anything in to clean it. Just wipe the outside.
SCA_MODELS.why: Analgesia as the mainstay, plus practical care of a perforated ear

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. How long will the gunk keep coming?
Usually a few days. If it keeps running once the infection has settled, or you think his hearing isn’t right once he’s better, I’ll want to look again to check the drum has healed.
SCA_MODELS.why: Sets the expected course and a follow-up trigger

SCA_MODELS.text: That makes sense.
Can I check it makes sense to you too? When someone at home asks what the doctor said, what will you tell them?
That his eardrum burst to let the pressure out, which is why he’s better, and it’ll heal. Regular Calpol or ibuprofen, keep it dry, and maybe antibiotics after you’ve looked.

Perfect. Now the important part. Call 999 or go to A&E if he becomes very drowsy or hard to wake, has a stiff neck, a rash that doesn’t fade under a glass, or is struggling to breathe. Come back the same day if a swelling or redness appears behind the ear or the ear sticks out, his face droops, he has a high temperature that won’t settle, or he stops drinking.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific plain-language red flags for meningitis, mastoiditis and facial palsy

SCA_MODELS.text: Behind the ear, stiff neck, rash, face — got it.

And if the antibiotic has been started and he’s not getting better after two or three days, ring us. You did the right thing calling. I’ll see you both this afternoon — anything else before we finish?
SCA_MODELS.why: Affirms the parent and closes with a clear plan

SCA_MODELS.text: No, that’s really helpful. Thank you.

SCA_STEM.name: Theo Marsh
pmh: No significant past medical history recorded
SCA_STEM.recent: Mother booked an urgent video appointment this morning: a few days of ear pain and a cold, then yellow discharge from one ear overnight. Now brighter in himself.
SCA_STEM.reason: Mother reports a “running ear” and is asking for antibiotics.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG91 (2018, updated 2022) — Otitis media (acute): antimicrobial prescribing · NICE NG143 (2019) — Fever in under 5s · NICE NG240 (2024) — Meningitis (bacterial) and meningococcal disease
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A discharging ear after a few days of earache is usually acute otitis media with a perforated drum. Assess well versus unwell first. Under NICE NG91, otorrhoea is one of the groups where an antibiotic is more likely to help, so no, back-up or immediate antibiotic are all reasonable options, chosen with the parent.

points.t: Temperature, colour, activity, hydration and breathing using the NICE NG143 traffic-light table in a febrile child under 5. Brighter, eating and playing is reassuring. Otoscopy is needed to confirm the diagnosis, so a video assessment is followed by a face-to-face examination.
Pain that eases suddenly as discharge appears suggests the drum has perforated and released pus. The perforation usually heals once the infection settles; recheck it if discharge persists.

NICE NG91: most children improve within about 3 days without antibiotics, though it can last up to a week. Offer paracetamol or ibuprofen at the dose for age or weight (BNFC). Anaesthetic ear drops (phenazone with lidocaine) are not used when the drum is perforated or the ear is discharging.

Immediate antibiotic for the systemically very unwell, signs of a more serious illness, or high risk of complications. For otorrhoea, or under 2 with both ears affected, consider no, back-up or immediate antibiotic — these groups benefit more. Otherwise no antibiotic or a back-up to use if not improving within 3 days or worse at any time.
NICE NG91: amoxicillin for 5 to 7 days, dose by age per NG91 and BNFC. Penicillin allergy: clarithromycin. Co-amoxiclav is the second choice if symptoms worsen after 2 to 3 days of the first choice.

NICE NG91: refer to hospital for a severe systemic infection or an acute complication — mastoiditis, meningitis, intracranial abscess, sinus thrombosis or facial nerve paralysis. Meningitis features follow NICE NG240; a febrile child with red features follows NICE NG143.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question to mother; noticed the child on screen; let her describe the pillow, the few days of earache and the antibiotic request in her own words.
Bad night, parental exhaustion and the wish to “do something”; can she attend in person today.
Picked up “he’s brighter now” as the key clinical cue and “I don’t want it spreading” as the key emotional cue, and explored both.
Idea (running ear = spreading infection); concern (it reaching his brain); expectation (antibiotics today).
NG143 traffic-light features by video, then face-to-face otoscopy, throat, chest and temperature; no swab needed routinely.
AOM with perforation versus otitis externa, and complications (mastoiditis, meningitis, facial palsy).
Checked behind the ear, neck stiffness, drowsiness, rash, facial weakness, hydration and breathing.
Acute otitis media with probable perforation in a systemically well child, confirmed on examination.
NG91 options for otorrhoea explained; shared decision on amoxicillin 5 to 7 days if confirmed; regular analgesia; keep the ear dry.
Checked allergy and high-risk conditions before prescribing; no decongestants, antihistamines or anaesthetic drops with a perforation.
999 features, same-day features, review if not improving in 2 to 3 days, and recheck the drum if discharge persists.

social.t: A frightening night drives the request. Acknowledging exhaustion and the wish to act builds trust faster than facts alone.
Keeping the ear dry (no swimming, care at bath time) and not cleaning inside the canal are practical points parents often miss.

legal.t: GMC Good practice in proposing, prescribing, providing and managing medicines and devices (2021): prescribe remotely only when you have enough information to do so safely; otherwise arrange an examination.

professional.t: NICE NG91 sets out when antibiotics help in acute otitis media. Following it — and explaining it — is good practice rather than rationing.
GMC Decision making and consent (2020): where more than one option is reasonable, share the choice with the parent and record the discussion and safety-net.

community.t: Pharmacists can advise on paracetamol and ibuprofen dosing for age and weight, and on when to seek further help.

redFlags: Swelling, redness or tenderness behind the ear, or the ear pushed forward (mastoiditis) — hospital
Drowsiness, neck stiffness, non-blanching rash, very unwell (meningitis) — 999
Facial weakness, or NG143 red traffic-light features in a febrile child under 5
psychosocial: A disturbed night for the whole family and an exhausted parent
Practical ability to attend today for examination
Past experience that may have taught her that discharge means antibiotics
ice: Idea: “A running ear means the infection is bursting out”
Concern: “It could spread to his brain”

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Acute otitis media with a probable perforated eardrum in a systemically well child. Confirm with otoscopy; NICE NG91 lists otorrhoea as a group where no, back-up or immediate antibiotic are all reasonable.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “The cold blocked the tube behind his eardrum and it filled with infected fluid. The pressure made a tiny hole in the drum, the fluid came out, and that’s why the pain eased. The hole almost always heals by itself.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried it was spreading — actually the discharge is his ear letting the pressure out, which is why he perked up. We’ll still keep a close eye for the rare signs that it is spreading.”
management.psychosocial: Acknowledge the bad night and the wish to do something; make the antibiotic decision together so mother leaves with a plan she owns, and arrange a convenient time for the examination.
sharedPlan: Face-to-face examination today: otoscopy, throat, chest, temperature
NG91 shared decision — amoxicillin 5 to 7 days if confirmed and chosen (dose by age per BNFC)
Regular paracetamol or ibuprofen; keep the ear dry; nothing inside the canal
safetyNet: 999: drowsy, stiff neck, non-blanching rash, breathing difficulty
Same day: swelling behind the ear, facial droop, persistent high fever, not drinking
Review if not improving in 2 to 3 days, or discharge or hearing concern persists

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station tests whether you can make an evidence-based antibiotic decision with a worried parent, not whether you know amoxicillin. Candidates fail it by refusing, by prescribing reflexively, or by forgetting that a video call cannot look inside an ear.

items.fail: Telling mother that antibiotics are never needed for ear infections.
items.why: NICE NG91 names otorrhoea as a group where antibiotics are more likely to help. A flat refusal is inaccurate management as well as poor relating.
items.fix: State the nuance: “Most ear infections settle alone, but with a discharging ear an antibiotic is a reasonable choice — let’s decide together.”

items.fail: Prescribing on the strength of “yellow gunk” without asking how the child is or arranging an examination.
items.why: “Did not assess the severity of illness” and “inadequate data gathering” are standard failing statements. Otitis externa and complications look different on examination.
items.fix: Ask about eating, drinking, playing and weeing, observe on camera, check behind the ear, then arrange same-day otoscopy.

items.fail: Treating “I don’t want it spreading” as a demand and answering it with statistics.
items.why: The fear of spread is the emotional hinge. Unexplored, it resurfaces as persistent requests however good the explanation.
items.fix: “What were you picturing when you saw the pillow?” — then explain the perforation as the answer to that fear.

items.fail: No pain-relief advice, or advising anaesthetic ear drops for a discharging ear.
items.why: NICE NG91 puts analgesia first, and phenazone with lidocaine drops are only for an intact drum without otorrhoea.
items.fix: Regular paracetamol or ibuprofen at the dose for age, dry-ear advice, nothing inside the canal.

items.fail: Closing with “come back if he gets worse”.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting fails the Global Skills domain; mastoiditis and meningitis are the complications examiners expect you to name.
items.fix: Name the signs: swelling behind the ear, a stiff neck, a rash that doesn’t fade, very drowsy, a drooping face — and give a review point at 2 to 3 days.

items.fail: Spending eight minutes on ear history and never reaching the decision.
items.why: “Management plan insufficiently developed” is the commonest reason for failing a station.
items.fix: Have the well/unwell picture by minute 4 and be explaining by minute 6.
